summary: The narrator, a filmmaker shooting on a New York street in the rain, is confronted by a Hispanic man who reveals a shoulder holster and a snub-nosed pistol and angrily tells him he is making a big mistake. Frightened, the narrator calls 911 and threatens to report the man to police over his problem with the New York film industry. The man walks off, possibly into a long black car that speeds toward Broadway. The narrator hides his fear from his crew member Arlene and reflects that the man must be connected to a phone call, though he cannot think of a serious reason anyone would be so worried about the shoot.
one_line: A filmmaker on a rainy New York shoot is confronted by an armed, menacing man who warns him off and then disappears.
key_facts: The narrator sees a shoulder holster under the jacket of his new Hispanic friend, containing a snub-nosed pistol.
The man bores in relentlessly on the narrator with eyes described as dead and merciless, saying "That is a big mistake."
The narrator says it is the first time in his life he has stood next to a man who had a gun and was deeply ticked at him.
The narrator says the man was not threatening him per se but letting him know how strongly he cared about what the narrator was doing.
The narrator compares the man to Nicky Russo, a figure who operated by an age-old set of Sicilian rules, and says this thug did not seem like the rule-book type.
With a shaking hand the narrator flicks open his cell phone and punches in 911.
The narrator tells the man that if he is threatening him with a gun, he is calling the cops, and that the man can explain his problem with the New York film industry to them.
New York's police emergency number was still ringing when the man abruptly turned and strode away.
The man seems to vanish into the rain, though someone who could have been him gets into a long black car down the block and speeds off toward Broadway.
Arlene asks what the creep wanted and comments that he looked like a heavy in one of David's old action pictures, needing only a Mack-10.
The narrator does not mention the gun to Arlene because he does not want to spook her.
The narrator plans to warn everybody to keep an eye out for strangers.
The narrator concludes the man was undoubtedly connected to the phone call but cannot think of any serious reason for anyone to be so worried about the shoot.
